nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet and essayist of the Romantic period writing under a pseudonym, and a lawyer who served as a metropolitan Commissioner in Lunacy
literary_identity: Lyric and dramatic poet of the Hunt school, who published as 'Barry Cornwall' to keep his professional reputation as a lawyer clear of his verse, and who became one of the most reprinted short-poem writers of mid-Victorian anthologies.
biography: Born at Leeds on 21 November 1787, the only son of the circuit barrister and public orator Bryan Procter, he was educated in the north and in London, entered a solicitor's office, and was called to the bar, where he practised as a special pleader. He began to publish verses about 1815 and came under the notice of Leigh Hunt, whose papers gave him a first public; in 1819 he issued 'Dramatic Scenes, and Other Poems', and the volumes that followed established him as a writer of simple, musical lyric and of dramatic verse for the closet. He was on terms of close friendship with Charles Lamb, whose letters to him are among the happiest documents of Regency letters, and with Hunt, Hazlitt, and the circle about the Indicator and the London Journal. From 1832 to 1861 he served as a metropolitan Commissioner in Lunacy, an office which gave his career its public shape and which he held while continuing to publish poems, essays, and literary-critical prose. His collected poetical works were reissued repeatedly, his lyrics entered the school and gift-book canon, and his songs and dramatic monologues were praised by Robert Browning and by the editors of household anthologies. He died on 5 October 1874.
literary_profile: His work is mostly short: songs and lyrics of quiet domestic or melancholy turn, dramatic scenes and monologues in the Elizabethan manner, metrical tales and legends of Italy and of the Cavalier period, and a few closet tragedies and sacred dramas. He wrote also prose essays and literary reminiscence, including papers on the old drama and on his friends, and his volumes of 1819-23 gathered the pieces by which Hunt's circle hoped to be read next after Byron.
stylistic_characteristics: Verse of deliberate plainness and song-like regularity: short lines, recurring refrains, and an affectation of old English and Cavalier music ('Cavalier Tones' is his best-known experiment in the manner). His dramatic poems take the monologue or the dialogue of two, with a prose-like directness of speech, and his prose is garrulous, affectionate, and anecdotal after Lamb.
intellectual_concerns: The persistence of the past in song and in domestic feeling; the pathos of private life and of the abandoned or betrayed woman; Elizabethan and Cavalier culture as an alternative to the high Romantic manner; the claims of professional respectability upon the literary life; madness, confinement, and the institutions charged with their care, which his official duties brought before him daily.
historical_significance: He marks the transmission of Hunt's 'new poets' programme into the mid-Victorian recital tradition: his lyrics and songs were staples of anthologies and of the household recitation that gave Romantic verse a popular afterlife. His friendships with Lamb, Hunt, and the Indicator circle make his work and papers a useful record of Regency literary society, and his career in the lunacy commission is a document of the professional Victorian man of letters.
major_influences: Charles Lamb's prose and friendship
Leigh Hunt's criticism and the Indicator's programme
Byron's and Rogers's lyrics
the Cavalier and Elizabethan songwriters
the old English drama
German-derived dramatic ballad

full_name: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; British peer, poet of the Romantic period, and a central figure of the European Romantic movement
literary_identity: Poet above all: writer of narrative and lyric verse, of metrical romances and tales, of verse satire in couplet and ottava rima, and of tragic poems designed for the reader rather than the playhouse; also the first modern literary celebrity, whose life was read as commentary on his work.
biography: Born 22 January 1788 in London, son of Captain 'Mad Jack' Byron (d. 1791) and Catherine Gordon of Aberdeen, he spent part of his childhood in Aberdeen before returning to England. In 1798 he inherited the barony and the embarrassed estate of Newstead Abbey, Nottinghamshire, from his great-uncle the fifth baron. He was at Harrow from 1801, where he wrote and circulated a great deal of school verse, and matriculated at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1805, withdrawing in 1808 without a degree. 'Hours of Idleness' was privately printed in 1807, and the hostile Edinburgh Review notice of its enlarged London issue drew from him the reply-satire 'English Bards and Scotch Reviewers' (1809). A journey to Portugal, Spain, Albania, and Greece with his companion John Cam Hobhouse (1809-11) supplied the matter of 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage', Cantos I-II, whose appearance in 1812 made his fame in a single season; he sat in the House of Lords, making his first speech against the Frame Bill in 1812. His marriage in January 1815 to Anneabella Milbanke ended in separation in January 1816 amid public scandal, and within months he left England for good, passing by Geneva and Lucerne to Venice (1816-19), Ravenna (1819-21), and Pisa and Genoa (1821-3), where he projected the monthly 'The Liberal' with Leigh Hunt and Percy Bysshe Shelley. In July 1823 he sailed to Greece for the war of independence, fell ill at Missolonghi in December, and died there on 19 April 1824 after repeated bloodletting; burial in Westminster Abbey being refused, he was laid in the Byron vault at Hucknall, Nottinghamshire.
literary_profile: His canon falls into three recognizable groups: the early satire and the romance tales in verse of 1813-16; the meditative-narrative 'Childe Harold' with the lyrics and short poems of the Italian exile; and the late work in which ottava rima and the tragic poem carry his most serious argument ('Beppo', 'Don Juan', 'Manfred', 'Cain', 'Heaven and Earth', the Venetian plays). He wrote no fiction of his own, no systematic criticism, and only prefatory and controversial prose, so his literary thought is best read in the poems, their advertisements and prefaces, and his letters and journals. His late verse tales and dramas in Greece and Italy were also the period's most spectacular commercial successes, and his letters and journals, edited after his death by Thomas Moore, became a foundational Romantic document.
stylistic_characteristics: Two contrasting manners in one voice: a high, sonorous descriptive rhetoric (Alpine, Adriatic, and Trojan scenery, apostrophe, the proud solitary speaker) and an urban, colloquial, laughing irony learned from Pope and from Italian ottava rima. He rhymes with ease and often with designed anticlimax, interrupts his own narrative to address the reader or publisher, and blends autobiographical confession with romance plot. In the dramas he aimed at a plain, passion-driven declamation and famously refused the 'poetry of description' for the stage.
intellectual_concerns: Liberty against tyranny, political and domestic; the guilt and self-fashioning of the outlawed aristocrat; scepticism toward revealed religion and sympathy with Milton's rebellious intellect; fame measured against its machinery of publishers and reviewers; sexual love, constancy, and betrayal; the rise and fall of states and dynasties; the capacity of irony to speak truth in a corrupt public culture.
historical_significance: He made the Romantic poet a European public person: 'Byron mania' swept British fashion, imitative verse tales, and the stage, while his example governed the second generation (Shelley's 'Adonais' and 'Epipsychidion' answer him), Pushkin and Lermontov, Mickiewicz, and the French Romantics. 'Don Juan' is the last great English poem in the Augustan satirical line and one of the first modern irony-driven long poems; his tragic poems and the Greek cause for which he died made him a liberal icon deep into the nineteenth century.
major_influences: Pope and the eighteenth-century verse satire
Johnsonian diction
the Bible and Milton
Wordsworth and Coleridge as models and as targets
Scott's metrical romances and the ballad revival
Italian narrative and comic verse (Ariosto, Pulci, Berni)
the gothic and oriental tale of the Minerva press
classical history and topography (Sallust, Cicero, the Troad)
his own Harrow and Aberdeen reading of romance and travel books
biographical_uncertainty: The precise grounds of the 1816 separation and the rumours of incest with his half-sister Augusta Leigh were suppressed in the family settlement and remain a matter of disputed interpretation; the paternity of his daughter Allegra was doubted in contemporary gossip and cannot be settled from the surviving evidence.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet, sketch-writer, and dramatist of the Romantic period, a member of the Hunt circle
literary_identity: Journalist-poet of the Examiner and the Indicator: writer of ballads, humorous tales in verse, sketches, and plays, and the friend to whom Keats addressed some of his most outgoing letters and verses.
biography: Born 9 September 1794 at Shrewsbury, he came to London as a young man and lived by literary and journalistic work. Leigh Hunt brought him into the circle of the Examiner and the Indicator, and through Hunt he met John Keats in October 1816; the two became inseparable during the years in which Keats was deciding to give up medicine, and Reynolds was the friend of Keats's most companionable poems, his sonnets, epistles, and the 'Epistle to John Hamilton Reynolds, during his excursion to the Leigh Hunt's'. He was one of the young writers attacked under the name of the 'cockney school', published ballads and tales in verse from about 1814, and in 1819 issued the continuation of Wordsworth's 'Peter Bell' which drew from Shelley a third part of his own. He contributed prose sketches, parodies, and plays of the comic and melodramatic kind through the 1820s and 1830s, wrote for the annuals and the magazines, and died on 15 November 1852. His later career lay outside the Romantic moment for which his friends remembered him, and his connection with Keats has often been allowed to stand for a larger body of work now little read.
literary_profile: Reynolds wrote in the mixed prose-and-verse idiom of the Hunt papers: narrative ballad and humorous metrical tale, the descriptive sketch, parody of the great style, and stage farce and drama of the minor theatres. His 'Peter Bell the Second' (1819) is the clearest surviving instance of the circle's method of poet-to-poet reply, and his essays and sonnets supply much of the evidence for the society of the Indicator and for the last years of Keats's life.
stylistic_characteristics: An easy, colloquial versifier of the Hunt school: ballad and anacreontic measures, pointed rhymes, a delight in parody of Wordsworthian and Byronic manner, and a prose of quick observation rather than argument. His sketches favour the first person, the anecdote, and the comic caricature of literary celebrities, and his dramatic pieces show the pull of the fashionable German-derived melodrama and of the Covent Garden and minor-theatre repertory.
intellectual_concerns: Friendship and companionship as the ground of literary life; the pleasures of the old English and Italian story told lightly; parody as a form of reading and of allegiance; the politics of the periodical press and the position of the unpatronised young writer; the theatre as a school of effect rather than of character.
historical_significance: His chief place in literary history is as the friend and interlocutor of Keats, whose letters to him (1817-21) are among the central documents of Romantic poetics and whose most companionable poems were written for or with him. His 'Peter Bell the Second' and Shelley's reply also map the circle's habit of competitive sequel-writing, and his journalism records the everyday texture of the Hunt papers between 1816 and 1822.
major_influences: Leigh Hunt's criticism and example
Wordsworth's narrative and 'Peter Bell'
Byron's tale in verse
the ballad and anacreontic tradition of the old English poets
German-derived melodrama and the comedy of the minor theatres
the daily and weekly paper war of the Regency
biographical_uncertainty: Reynolds's education and early employment, the chronology of his contributions to the Examiner and the Indicator, and the dates of his several plays and collections are imperfectly documented, and his share in pieces written jointly with Keats in 1819 is still debated.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet of the Romantic period, member of the Hunt circle and the target of the 'cockney school' label applied by the quarterly reviews
literary_identity: Poet only: sonneteer, writer of the long romance 'Endymion', of metrical tales, and of the great odes and 'Hyperion' poems of 1819; a medically trained man who gave up practice for verse, and a letter-writer whose phrases ('negative capability', 'soul-making') entered the period's documented criticism.
biography: Born 31 October 1795 in London, eldest child of a livery-stable keeper, he was orphaned young: his father died of a fall from a horse in 1804 and his mother of consumption in 1810, leaving the children in the guardianship of the surgeon Richard Abbey. He was educated at John Clarke's school at Enfield, where he read Chapman's Homer, Spenser, and the modern histories with a schoolboy's appetite, was bound apprentice in 1810 to the surgeon-apothecary Thomas Hammond at Edmonton, and trained at Guy's Hospital from 1815, qualifying as an apothecary in 1816 before abandoning medicine the following year to live by verse. Leigh Hunt brought him into the circle of the Examiner and the Indicator in October 1816, introducing him to his brothers, to John Hamilton Reynolds, to Woodhouse, Haydon, and Shelley; 'O Solitude' was printed in the Examiner on 5 May 1816, and the Chapman sonnet in the same paper that December. The volume 'Poems' appeared on 3 March 1817 and 'Endymion: A Poetic Romance' in 1818, and the attacks on both in Blackwood's Magazine and the Quarterly Review fixed the 'cockney' warfare that shadowed his career. In 1818 he walked in the Lake District and with Reynolds in Scotland, nursed his brother Tom, who died of consumption that December, and fell in love with Fanny Brawne at Hampstead. At Wentworth Place in 1819 he wrote 'Isabella', 'The Eve of St. Agnes', 'Lamia', the Hyperion poems, and the spring odes; with health failing and marriage impossible he sailed for Italy with Joseph Severn in September 1820 and died near the Piazza di Spagna in Rome on 23 February 1821, aged twenty-five. He lies in the Protestant Cemetery at Rome under the stone he dictated, recording only that here lies one whose name was writ in water.
literary_profile: His output is short and dense: the early Spenserian and Homeric exercises, the 1816-18 sonnets, epistles, and 'Sleep and Poetry'; the four-book romance 'Endymion'; the metrical tales 'Isabella' and 'Lamia' and the romance 'The Eve of St. Agnes'; the two Hyperion poems; the odes of 1819 with 'To Autumn' and the late lyrics; and two unfinished attempts in tragedy and dramatic sketch. His prose letters - to Reynolds, to Woodhouse, to Bailey, to the Dilkes and Woodleys, and to Severn from Rome - carry his most quoted critical statements on negative capability, the poetical character's want of self, and the world as a vale of soul-making.
stylistic_characteristics: Sensation rendered as texture: heavy sensory concreteness, compound epithets, synaesthesia, and a slow, vowel-weighted music; an insistence on the palpable image that stays before the senses instead of resolving into argument. He rebuilt the English ode in stanzas of his own devising, handled the Spenserian and Elizabethan stanza and the Italian romance stanza with a romantic ear, and turned the sonnet into a vehicle of high statement about poetry, mortality, and the imagination.
intellectual_concerns: Identity and the dissolution of the self in other existences (negative capability); the agonistic love of the old poets - Chapman, Spenser, Shakespeare, Milton; beauty, truth, and the evidence of the imagination; early death, consumption, and the endurance of verse; the ethics of making in a reviewing market that punished ambition of humble origin; the Hellenic world as a school of form; the search for a theodicy without theology in the 'vale of Soul-making'.
historical_significance: Within a decade of his death he had become one of the most reprinted poets in English, and the 1819 ode sequence set the model for later aesthetic and sensualist traditions. His letters made him the Romantic period's most quoted theorist of imagination and selflessness; the 'cockney' attacks on him sharpened the class war in Romantic letters, and his death at twenty-five in Rome fixed the enduring myth of the early-martyred poet which Shelley's 'Adonais' first consecrated and which Hunt's and Woodhouse's papers afterwards preserved.
major_influences: Chapman's Homer and the Elizabethan translators
Spenser
Shakespeare's sonnets and late plays
Milton and the solemn high style
Leigh Hunt's liberality and example
Haydon's paintings and the Elgin sculpture
the Wordsworthian sonnet
the ballad and romance tradition
Boccaccio as retold in French and English novelle for 'Isabella'
the anatomical and clinical training at Guy's Hospital and its culture of close observation
biographical_uncertainty: The exact course of his last illness (consumption, with a fatal haemorrhage, aggravated by the treatment he received) and the weight of the hostile criticism in hastening his decline were argued from 1821 onward and remain matters of interpretation rather than record; the dates of his engagement to Fanny Brawne are better documented than the later legend that he died of a broken heart.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet, essayist, editor, and critic of the Romantic period, the manager and chief theorist of the Hunt circle
literary_identity: Essayist and editor first, poet next: the conductor of the Examiner and the Indicator whose prose, criticism, and personal patronage made possible much of the verse of 1814-1822, and whose own romantic narratives and lyrical sketches were read as a manifesto of a poetry free from the neoclassical school.
biography: Born 19 October 1784 in London, son of a Philadelphia-born lawyer of Puritan stock who had been disinherited for his Loyalism and of an English mother, he was put to work young and became a clerk in the Receiver General's office before turning to journalism. With his younger brother John he founded the Examiner in 1808, and through the Reflector (1810-11) and the weekly Indicator he built the paper into the organ of a literary as well as a political party. His prosecution for libel on the Prince Regent in 1812 and his two-year imprisonment made him a liberal martyr and drew to him Byron, Shelley, Keats, Hazlitt, and Reynolds; in prison and after it he wrote 'The Story of Rimini' (1816), which Hunt's circle took as the model of a new simplicity drawn from Boccaccio and the old English tales. He introduced Keats to Shelley, published the sonnets of 1816-17, and lent his name and his press to the poetry which the Quarterly and Edinburgh reviews afterwards grouped as the 'cockney school'. Invited by Byron to join the projected 'Liberal', he sailed for Italy in 1821, edited the magazine through its three numbers with Byron's poems and Shelley's, and remained abroad until 1825, enduring the collapse of the enterprise and the deaths and quarrels it had gathered. Back in London he revived his editorial career (the London Journal of 1828), published his controversial 'Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries' (1828), and wrote on drama, poetry, and the arts until his death on 28 August 1859; his 'Autobiography', published in 1850-56, became a primary document of the period he had helped to make.
literary_profile: His work divides into the light narrative and descriptive verse ('The Feast of the Poets', 'Rimini', the sonnets and sketches of the Indicator), the familiar prose of the periodical essay and of criticism on poetry and the theatre, and the memoir and biographical writing of the later years. He was also, practically, an editor and manager: the Examiner's literary page, the Indicator's papers on the old poets, and the 'Liberal' are literary works in the collective sense, and their policy of publishing young and unpopular verse shaped the period's canon.
stylistic_characteristics: A prose of ease, intimacy, and apparent unpremeditation - short sentences, parentheses, the tone of a friend talking in a room - concealing a deliberate theory of 'spontaneity' and of the 'love of beauty for its own sake'. His verse prefers the easy narrative stanza, the familiar sonnet, and the descriptive sketch, with an Italian and Elizabethan secondhand music and a fondness for the tale of illicit tenderness; his criticism quotes rather than argues.
intellectual_concerns: The emancipation of poetry from neoclassical decorum and from party patronage; the literary public sphere and its economics of reviews and magazines; political libel and the price of a free press; Italian and old English literature as a school of romantic feeling; the fellowship of poets against the 'thundering' school; the biography and gossip of literary fame as evidence of character; sensibility and its enjoyment, defended against the charge of coarseness.
historical_significance: No single figure did more to create the institutional conditions of the second generation of English Romanticism: he discovered or advertised Keats, published and defended Shelley, supplied Byron with the tale of Rimini and with the Liberal, and with Hazlitt and Lamb defined the familiar critic's voice for the century's periodical writing. His imprisonment, the reviews' war on the 'cockney school', and the ruin of the Liberal enterprise are also the best documented case of politics and personality acting on Romantic literary reputation.
major_influences: The eighteenth-century familiar essay (Addison and Sterne)
Eliza and the old dramatists read in his brother's theatre-going
Boccaccio and the Italian novellieri
Chaucer, Spenser, and the Elizabethan lyric
Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads as both pattern and provocation
the liberal journalism of the morning papers
his father's American Puritan inheritance and its anecdotal culture
biographical_uncertainty: The extent of his own responsibility for the Examiner's most provocative passages, and the fairness of his later charges against Byron and against Moore's editing of Byron, are contested; his account of his own precedence in the 'Rimini' quarrel and in the discovery of Keats must be read against the records of the reviews and of his brothers' papers.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet and prose polemicist of the Romantic period, the most systematically radical of the major Romantic writers
literary_identity: Poet of philosophical narrative poems, of the lyric and ode, and of verse drama written for the reader rather than the manager; also an essayist on poetry, atheism, diet, and reform whose polemic is inseparable from his verse.
biography: Born 4 August 1792 at Field Place in Sussex, eldest son of Timothy Shelley (later second baronet) and Elizabeth Pilfold, he was educated at Syon House, at Eton (1804-10), where he wrote the gothic romances 'Zastrozzi' (1810) and 'St. Irvyne' (1811), and at University College, Oxford, from 1810. In March 1811 he and Thomas Jefferson Hogg were expelled for refusing to answer for the pamphlet 'The Necessity of Atheism', and in the same year he ran off to Scotland with the sixteen-year-old Harriet Westbrook, whom he married. He intervened in Irish agitation in 1812, privately printed 'Queen Mab' in 1813, and in July 1814 eloped to the Continent with Mary Godwin, daughter of William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft. The 1816 summer at the Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva, with Byron and Claire Clairmont, produced 'Hymn to Intellectual Beauty' and 'Mont Blanc' and the germ of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. Harriet Shelley's suicide in December 1816 cleared the way for his marriage to Mary, but their position in England became untenable and the family moved to Italy in March 1818; the deaths of the children Clara (1818) and William (1819) and the loss of the guardianship suit over Percy Florence deepen the grief of the great years 1819-20, which yielded 'Prometheus Unbound', 'The Cenci', the west wind and skylark odes, and 'Peter Bell the Third'. At Pisa in 1821 he wrote 'Adonais' for Keats, and his alliance with Leigh Hunt brought out the monthly 'The Liberal' (1822). He was drowned on 8 July 1822 when his boat 'Bolivar' went down in a storm in the Gulf of La Spezia on the return from Livorno; his ashes lie in the Protestant Cemetery at Rome beside Keats.
literary_profile: His work moves from schoolboy gothic prose to the long philosophical poem ('Queen Mab', 'Alastor', 'Laon and Cythna'), and then to the mature compact of lyric, elegy, and drama in Italy ('Prometheus Unbound', the odes of 1820, 'Adonais', 'Epipsychidion', 'Hellas', 'The Triumph of Life'). A parallel prose body - 'A Defence of Poetry', 'The Necessity of Atheism', 'A Philosophical View of Reform', 'A Vindication of Natural Diet', the 'Letter to Maria Gisborne' and the letters from Italy - states the doctrine that poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. Much of it went unpublished or appeared piratically in his lifetime, and his canon was largely made posthumous by Mary Shelley's editions of 1824 and after.
stylistic_characteristics: An eloquence of transference: abstractions personified, natural agencies made emblems of mind, and verse periods that lengthen and recur within intricate stanzas ('The Cloud', 'Ode to the West Wind'). He adapts Italian and English forms with self-conscious formal experiment - terza rima, the Spenserian-like stanzas of 'Laon and Cythna', the complex stanzette of 'Adonais', the tailless lyric stanza of 'To a Skylark' - and his prose is argumentative, lucid, and frequently turns into manifesto.
intellectual_concerns: Necessity and the ethics of reform; atheism, freethought, and the critique of revealed religion; sexual love, free marriage, and the equal claim of women; diet, medicine, and the perfectibility of the body; imagination as a way of knowing and poetry as the engine of moral change; the tyranny of priest, king, and established opinion, tested against the French revolution, Greek freedom, and Italian despotism; death, mourning, and the survival of the poet's thought.
historical_significance: He bequeathed to later radicals and aesthetes a single powerful idea - that poetry reforms the mind which law cannot reach - which made him the hero of Chartists, of the freethought press of the 1820s-1890s, and of twentieth-century radical literary history. 'Prometheus Unbound' and the Italian lyrics rewrote the Miltonic and Wordsworthian inheritance, and 'A Defence of Poetry' remains a founding document of the autonomous-poetry tradition.
major_influences: William Godwin's political justice and doctrine of necessity
Mary Wollstonecraft's vindication of women's claims
Plato and the symposium of ideal love
Lucretius and atomist natural philosophy
Rousseau and the confessional tradition
Wordsworth's great Ode and 'The Excursion'
Spenser's 'Mutabilitie' cantos
Milton's Satan and the dramatic sublime
Dante and Petrarch (terza rima and the triumph tradition)
Greek lyric and tragedy read in translation
Erasmus Darwin and Humphry Davy's chemical lecture culture
